text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed higher in quiet trade. Neither Czarnikow's first estimate of world sugar production 1997/98 nor our first estimate of European beet sugar production had any impact on world market prices, as both estimates were in line with expectations. October added $1.70 to close at $324.20 per tonne, while December closed $1.90 higher at $321.60 per tonne.

Raw sugar futures in New York closed higher on the day but prices remained slack in their recent trading range with no fundamental news to inspire any significant movement. October closed 6 points higher at 11.55 cents/lb, while March added 3 points to close at 11.78 cents/lb. The outer months gained between 4 and 6 points. It will need some strong fundamental change to push prices out of their current trading range.

C. CZARNIKOW - In its latest market report London trade house C. Czarnikow has put world sugar production in 1997/98 at 123.3 million tonnes, slightly up from last year's figure of 123.1 million tonnes. Czarnikow said that it is interesting to note that the three latest crops are all within 0.25 million tonnes of each other after the sharp surge in 1995/96. However, this apparent flat rate of production over the three seasons masks the huge decline that has taken place in India where the crop has dropped by 6.2 million tonnes, raw value. The other side of the coin is that despite the scale of this decline, there have been counter-balancing gains elsewhere in the world, with Brazil expanding by 2 million tonnes, the EU by 1 million, and increases also in South Africa, China, Mexico, Australia, Pakistan and Turkey amongst many others, Czarnikow said.

The company added that consumption continues to move ahead and that the total in calendar year 1998 could be 124.4 million tonnes, up from 122.0 million tonnes in 1997 and 119.7 million tonnes in 1996. Czarnikow said one of the main driving forces for growth over many years has been the demand in Asia and in particular the Far East. A number of the countries in the region have found problems springing to the surface this year and it remains to be seen whether the previous rate of increase will be checked for a while. Czarnikow estimates unrecorded consumption at 750,000 tonnes and when this is added to consumption, Czarnikow's estimates point to a draw down of stocks in the coming cycle of 1.87 million tonnes. This compares with a revised increase in stocks estimated for 1996/97 of 0.37 million tonnes.

IRELAND - Sugar exports in March 1997 amounted to 19,172 tonnes, raw value, up from 6,025 tonnes in March 1996. This brought cumulative exports in the first half of 1996/97 (October/March) up to 41,702 tonnes compared to 51,392 tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total exports in 1995/96 amounted to 74,907 tonnes compared to 56,773 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of destination in 1996/97 were the UK with 22,263 tonnes whites against 25,253 tonnes and Pakistan with 14,000 tonnes compared to nil.

MALAYSIA - Sugar imports in May 1997 reached 96,900 tonnes, raw value, unchanged from the shipments in May 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first five months of 1997 up to 433,507 tonnes against 416,167 tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1996 reached 1.093 million tonnes against 1.033 million tonnes in 1995. Major countries of origin in 1997 were Thailand with 261,750 tonnes raws against 294,800 tonnes, Australia with 138,422 tonnes against 121,367 tonnes and Colombia with 19,000 tonnes compared to nil.

Sugar exports in January/May 1997 amounted to 32,777 tonnes against 45,244 tonnes in the corresponding period the previous year. Total exports in 1996 reached 115,937 tonnes compared to 123,561 tonnes in 1995. Major countries of destination in 1997 were Singapore with 18,189 tonnes whites against 26,160 tonnes and Indonesia with 6,443 tonnes, down from 12,069 tonnes.
